source.title: Codebook Features: Sparse and Discrete Interpretability for Neural Networks
source.authors: Alex Tamkin; Mohammad Taufeeque; Noah D. Goodman

record.tranche_reason: Tests the superposition explanation in a controlled finite-state task using code purity and code-versus-neuron classification, rather than reproducing the original neuron-visualization method.
record.gate_note: The paper reports code-versus-neuron feature-classification results and layerwise code-purity results relevant to superposition. Topic-steering outcomes are deliberately induced and do not measure spontaneous neuron polysemanticity; model-performance results do not measure the claim. The WikiText comparison does not estimate the share of polysemantic neurons or test layerwise differences, so it is recorded under fits_no_version.
record.test_reason: The paper takes superposition as its motivation and reports how well its own codebook method works: code purity, and code-vs-best-neuron classifier precision. It never measures how common polysemantic neurons are. It never varies the ratio of features to neurons, activation function or architecture to test why neurons are polysemantic. The neuron comparisons pit the authors' method against neurons in a codebook-finetuned network, which is a method-performance comparison, not a test of any version.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors conclude that codebook bottlenecks give sparse, discrete, interpretable features with modest performance loss. In the FSM setting, codes represent more features than there are neurons and 'mitigate superposition'. Codes can also be steered causally. They note that codes merge states with similar next-token distributions in later layers, and that many codes in larger models are not interpretable.
record.recipe_differences: The paper trains codebook-bottleneck networks and compares code-based feature classification and purity with neuron-based classification; it does not reproduce the original neuron visualization method.
record.method_sensitivity: In the TokFSM codebook model, code purity declines in higher MLP layers. The study also reports code-versus-neuron classifier comparisons on TokFSM and WikiText-103, but does not measure polysemantic-neuron prevalence across layers.

fits_no_version.finding: In the TokFSM codebook model (128 neurons per MLP layer, 100 states), the best single neuron at each state code's recall averages 70.5% precision, against 97.1% for codes. The authors say anecdotally that neuron top-activating tokens show no consistent pattern.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In a small transformer on a synthetic FSM task, single neurons are imperfect detectors of known latent states compared with learned sparse codes.

fits_no_version.finding: In a Pythia-410M model finetuned with codebooks on WikiText-103, codes beat the best neuron at matched recall by over 30% average precision. The regex features were selected because codes looked interpretable.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: On regex-targeted features selected via codes, sparse codes outperform the best single neuron as classifiers.

record.problems: The language-model neuron comparison is preliminary: regular expressions are imperfect proxies, and selecting codes with interpretable patterns may bias the comparison in their favor. Exact values for the layerwise purity curves are shown only in a figure. The paper does not estimate the prevalence of polysemantic neurons in language models.
record.rows_left_out: No other claim-relevant measured results were left out. Language-model steering results concern deliberately activated codes, and codebook model performance results do not measure neuron polysemanticity.

untested.parts: No share of polysemantic MLP neurons is estimated, and no layer comparison of neurons is made in language models.
The ratio of features to neurons is not manipulated, and neuron polysemanticity is not linked causally to capacity.
There is no test of polysemanticity arising from initialization, regularization or noise when capacity is sufficient.
Neuron polysemanticity is not compared across activation functions or architectures.
No canonical polysemantic neurons are re-examined.
Neuron polysemanticity is not compared across activation ranges or scoring methods.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's link of R1–R9 to V3 was wrong. The purity rows measure codes, not neurons. The neuron comparisons are the study's method compared against neurons inside a codebook-finetuned network. Superposition is assumed as framing, not tested.

versions.untested_parts: No image classifier or InceptionV1 neurons are analyzed.
The language-model classifier comparison does not estimate the share of MLP neurons responding to unrelated tokens or contexts, or compare that share across layers.
Tested in the controlled TokFSM setting using codebook representations and neuron comparisons; not tested across ordinary language-model neurons or other networks.
No test of polysemanticity arising from initialization, regularization, or training noise when capacity is sufficient.
No comparison of the share of polysemantic neurons across activation functions, architectures, or regularization methods, and no SoLU or modern-convnet comparison.
The paper does not re-examine canonical polysemantic neurons to determine whether their mixed inputs share a coherent feature.
No comparison of neuron polysemanticity under different activation ranges or explanation-scoring methods.

rows.subject: TokFSM k=1 Attn+MLP codebook model
rows.operation_detail: Compared code-classifier precision with the best neuron precision at matched recall for state classification.

conditions.value: matched between code and neuron classifiers

rows.note: The authors compare code classifiers with the best neuron at the same recall and describe code precision as far better. The FSM has 100 states; the network's hidden size is 128.
rows.check: This compares the study's own method (codes) with neurons. Best-neuron precision of 70.5% at the code's recall shows neurons are imperfect state classifiers. It does not test whether polysemanticity is caused by more features than neurons: capacity is not varied, and the 100 states are fewer than the 128 neurons.

rows.subject: TokFSM k=1 Attn+MLP codebook model
rows.operation_detail: Measured fraction of pure MLP codes, defined as codes activating on only one state for bigrams or one state-plus-first-digit for trigrams.
rows.measure: Fraction of codes that are pure
rows.note: The text describes very high purity and says the first layer mostly resolves superposition; exact plotted value is not stated.
rows.check: This measures the purity of learned codes, not neurons, so it says nothing about neuron polysemanticity or its cause. The authors' phrase 'resolves superposition' describes their method.

rows.stage_stated: finetuned on WikiText-103 from a pretrained Pythia model
rows.operation_detail: Compared code-classifier precision with the best neuron precision at matched recall for selected regular-expression features.

conditions.value: selected interpretable linguistic features, targeted by regular expressions
matched between code and neuron classifiers

rows.measure: Average precision across selected feature classifiers
rows.value: Codes had over 30% higher average precision than neurons
rows.note: The paper says it exhaustively searches all 410 million neurons for the best performer. This comparison does not report the share of polysemantic neurons or test the superposition mechanism in the sense of V3.
rows.check: This compares the method with neurons on regex features chosen to fit codes. It gives no share of polysemantic neurons.

reader_labels.condition: TokFSM code-versus-neuron state classification and first-layer code purity
reader_labels.reason: Codes classify states at 97.1% average precision versus 70.5% for the average best neuron, and first-layer codes are described as very pure; see R1–R3.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
